alignment.note: Greek pairs the conjunction καί with the aorist participle εἰσελθών ('and having entered'); the Vulgate mirrors this with et + the participle ingressus. The Peshitta condenses both into a single coordinated finite verb ܘܥܠ ('and he entered'), preferring paratactic finite verbs to participial subordination, a typical Syriac stylistic choice.
λέγει / ܘܐܡܪ / ait, though the Syriac again prefixes the coordinating waw.

The dative pronoun (αὐτοῖς / ܠܗܘܢ / illis) agrees across all three; the Vulgate isolates the following discourse with an explicit colon (token 4), a punctuation feature absent from the unpointed Greek and Syriac text streams here treated as part of the preceding clause.

Greek θορυβεῖσθε and Latin turbamini are synthetic medio-passive 2nd-person plural forms; the Peshitta employs an analytic construction, the active participle ܪܗܝܒܝܢ plus the enclitic pronoun ܐܢܬܘܢ ('you are agitated'), the normal Syriac strategy for present-tense person marking.
καί / ܘ- / et, here joining the two predicates.

Greek κλαίετε and Latin ploratis are finite 2nd-person plural verbs; the Peshitta uses the participle ܒܟܝܢ governed by the single shared enclitic ܐܢܬܘܢ from the prior clause, and the Vulgate alone marks the interrogative force with a closing question mark (token 9).

Greek uses the neuter diminutive τὸ παιδίον ('the little child') with the article; the Vulgate renders puella ('girl'), specifying feminine gender, and the Peshitta ܛܠܝܬܐ likewise is the feminine 'little girl,' both versions making explicit the female sex left grammatically neuter in the Greek diminutive.

Greek ἀπέθανεν is a simple aorist indicative; the Peshitta ܡܝܬܬ is a finite perfect (feminine, agreeing with the girl); the Vulgate builds a periphrastic perfect est mortua ('has died/is dead'), distributing the sense over copula plus participle.

Greek καθεύδει and Latin dormit are single finite present verbs; the Peshitta uses the participle ܕܡܟܐ plus the enclitic feminine pronoun ܗܝ ('she is sleeping'), again preferring the analytic participle-plus-pronoun present typical of Syriac and agreeing with the feminine subject.
